value.overview: The White-collared Manakin is a small, lively forest bird of the manakin family. Males are strikingly patterned in black, olive-green, yellow, and white, while females and young birds are mostly olive-green with yellow underparts. It is best known for communal courtship displays in which males clear small patches on the forest floor and produce loud wing-snapping sounds. The species commonly uses dense forest edges, secondary growth, and other thick vegetation.
value.classification: The White-collared Manakin belongs to the manakin family, Pipridae, in the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Manacus candei.
value.identification: Adults are about 11 centimeters long. The adult male has a black crown, black wings and tail, an olive-green back and rump, a bright yellow belly, and a conspicuous white collar and throat. Females, immature males, and juveniles are duller olive-green above with yellowish underparts and lack the male’s bold black-and-white pattern. In Costa Rica, female-type birds can resemble other manakins, but range and habitat help separate them from related species.
value.rangeHabitat: The White-collared Manakin ranges from southeastern Mexico through Central America to western Panama. In Costa Rica it is primarily a resident of the Caribbean lowlands and foothills, generally from sea level to about 700 meters. It occurs in humid forest edges, dense thickets along streams, tall secondary growth, and old cacao plantations. It may reach the Pacific side locally through low passes in the Cordillera de Guanacaste, but Pacific-slope populations are largely represented by related manakin species.
value.migrationStatus: Resident and essentially non-migratory in Costa Rica. Individuals remain in suitable lowland and foothill habitats year-round, although local movements may occur as birds track fruiting vegetation or suitable dense cover.
value.breeding: Males gather at communal display sites, or leks, on the forest floor. Each male clears a small circular court and jumps between thin upright sticks while producing sharp wing snaps; males may also raise their throat feathers into a beard-like ruff. The female builds a shallow cup nest, usually 1–3 meters above the ground in a horizontal fork. She incubates the eggs and cares for the young alone, because adults do not form lasting breeding pairs.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on small fruits gathered from low and middle levels of vegetation. It also takes insects and other small arthropods, often catching them from foliage during short flights. White-collared Manakins may forage in loose, scattered groups, with males periodically giving wing snaps or displaying nearby. Their fruit-based diet makes them useful seed dispersers in forest edges and regenerating woodland.
value.behavior: White-collared Manakins are active, agile birds that usually stay within dense lower vegetation. Males are especially conspicuous during the breeding season because of their coordinated lek displays, jumping movements, throat-feather displays, and loud wing snaps. Outside display activity, the birds can be difficult to see, moving quickly through tangles while feeding. They often occur in small, loosely organized groups rather than in stable pairs.

conservation.populationTrend: Generally considered stable at the global level.
